name: Vanadium
role: Alternative nitrogenase and microbial vanadium reduction

summary.text: Vanadium has a defined cofactor role in certain nitrogen-fixing microbes. Other bacteria transform vanadium between oxidation states, making it relevant to both enzyme chemistry and environmental metal cycling.

mechanisms.text: Azotobacter vinelandii vanadium nitrogenase contains an iron-vanadium cofactor and catalyzes nitrogen reduction. Its cofactor differs structurally from the molybdenum-containing form.
Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 reduced V(V) to V(IV) through an electron-transfer pathway involving menaquinone and membrane cytochromes.

Growth on vanadate depends on culture conditions: a 2004 study observed reduction without growth, while a 2005 study demonstrated proton translocation and growth after modifying the medium. Reduction alone therefore does not establish energy conservation.

microbiome.text: The selected evidence concerns environmental bacteria, enzyme structures, and laboratory metal reduction. It does not establish a vanadium-dependent human gut function or a validated vanadium-associated disease signature.

exposure.text: Vanadate and reduced vanadium species are chemically distinct microbial exposures. Enzyme-bound vanadium is also different from dissolved vanadium added to a culture.

limits.text: Vanadium is not a universal microbial requirement. Claims about metabolism must identify the organism, oxidation state, and experimental conditions.

name: Manganese
role: Oxidative-stress defense and environmental manganese cycling

summary.text: Manganese can support microbial resistance to oxidative stress, while its accessibility is contested by the host. Environmental microbes also transform manganese oxidation states, linking microbial energy metabolism to mineral formation.

mechanisms.text: Calprotectin-mediated manganese restriction impaired Staphylococcus aureus superoxide defenses and increased susceptibility to neutrophil killing in experimental infection work.
A two-species enrichment culture grew by coupling Mn(II) oxidation to carbon fixation, providing experimental evidence for manganese-based chemolithoautotrophy.
In mice, a high-manganese diet increased manganese availability in the heart and promoted S. aureus infection there, demonstrating tissue-specific consequences of metal access.

microbiome.text: The cited host studies address a defined pathogen and experimental infection, not a general human gut dysbiosis signature. The environmental culture result demonstrates manganese-supported growth, not a mechanism of human neurological disease.

exposure.text: Dietary manganese was manipulated in the mouse infection study; Mn(II) was the energy substrate in the environmental enrichment culture. These are different exposure systems and should be labeled separately.

limits.text: Metal availability at a specific tissue can differ from total dietary intake. Neither the mouse infection model nor environmental oxidation experiments establish a human microbiome-mediated disease pathway.

name: Iron
role: Iron acquisition, iron-sulfur enzymes, and environmental respiration

summary.text: Iron connects intracellular enzyme chemistry with competition for nutrients and environmental redox cycling. Its biological availability depends on its oxidation state, ligands, and mineral form; measuring total iron alone does not describe what a microbe can access.

mechanisms.text: Siderophores capture iron. Host lipocalin 2 binds the bacterial siderophore enterobactin, while the iroA-associated salmochelin pathway can evade this defense in experimental E. coli systems.
Iron-sulfur clusters support bacterial metabolism and can be damaged by competing metals. In E. coli, copper inactivated iron-sulfur dehydratases without requiring oxygen.

In anaerobic culture, the sediment isolate GS-15 coupled organic carbon oxidation to Fe(III) reduction and growth. Amorphous oxides and dissolved ferric citrate behaved differently from highly crystalline iron minerals.

microbiome.text: Human intervention evidence exists: two randomized trials involving 115 Kenyan infants found that iron-containing micronutrient powders increased several enterobacterial measures and fecal calprotectin in that setting. The result concerns particular formulations, infant populations, and exposure conditions; it is not a universal effect of every dietary iron source.

exposure.text: Relevant interfaces include iron in food fortification and iron-bearing sediment minerals. The fraction reaching the colon and the chemical form of environmental iron matter for microbial access.

limits.text: Host iron status, microbial strain, inflammation, formulation, and local chemistry change the interpretation. An increased taxon's relative abundance does not identify the intracellular iron concentration or prove a disease mechanism.

name: Cobalt
role: Corrinoid sharing, vitamin B12 uptake, and metal interference

summary.text: Cobalt is central to cobalamin and related corrinoids, which form a shared but chemically diverse resource in microbial communities. Free cobalt exposure is a different biological question from access to intact vitamin B12 or its analogs.

mechanisms.text: Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron carries several corrinoid transporters with distinct preferences. Individual transporters changed competitive fitness in gnotobiotic mice depending on the corrinoids available.

In E. coli, excess cobalt disrupted iron-sulfur enzyme function. Biochemical experiments implicated interference with cluster assembly on scaffold proteins rather than direct attack on fully assembled clusters.

microbiome.text: The corrinoid study combined analysis of human gut microbial genomes with culture experiments and colonization of germ-free mice. It demonstrates how vitamin uptake specificity can shape competition, without establishing that cobalt salts and cobalamin have equivalent effects on a human microbiome.

exposure.text: Corrinoids may be available from diet or microbial production; the chemical structure influences which organisms can capture them. Cobalt-ion culture exposure instead probes metal toxicity.

limits.text: Corrinoid dependence varies between organisms and metabolic pathways. Benefits inferred from vitamin-dependent microbial enzymes cannot be transferred to free cobalt exposure.

summary.text: Nickel supports distinct microbial enzyme systems, including urease and [NiFe]-hydrogenases. Some glyoxalase I enzymes prefer nickel, but that property is not shared by all glyoxalase I proteins; metal identity must be established for the organism and enzyme in question.

mechanisms.text: H. pylori uses nickel-dependent urease and hydrogenase during gastric colonization. Histidine-rich Hpn and Hpn-like proteins store nickel, helping the bacterium maintain access when external supply is limited.

Purified E. coli glyoxalase I showed optimal activation by Ni(II), unlike the familiar zinc-activated enzymes from several other organisms. The work concerns methylglyoxal-processing enzyme biochemistry.
In E. coli, the nickel-responsive regulator NikR represses the NikABCDE import system, linking intracellular nickel sensing to uptake control.
Accessory proteins coordinate nickel delivery: H. pylori HypA and UreG competed for UreE binding in biochemical experiments, revealing interactions between hydrogenase and urease maturation pathways.

microbiome.text: Mouse colonization experiments showed that H. pylori nickel-storage mutants were disadvantaged on nickel-deficient chow, whereas wild-type colonization was similar across the tested diets. This supports a specific pathogen-storage mechanism rather than a claim that higher dietary nickel universally increases colonization.

exposure.text: Dietary nickel was experimentally controlled in the H. pylori mouse work. Enzyme assays and transporter studies used defined nickel conditions, which do not directly represent a mixed human diet.

limits.text: These studies do not demonstrate that nickel-dependent enzymes cause endometriosis or Parkinson's disease. Presence of an enzyme gene also does not establish its expression, metal occupancy, or activity in a patient's microbiome.

name: Copper
role: Methane oxidation, copper acquisition, and metal toxicity

summary.text: Copper supports specialized microbial chemistry while excess accessible copper damages sensitive cellular targets. Its microbial roles span methane-oxidizing environmental bacteria and the metal-defense systems of organisms such as E. coli.

mechanisms.text: Methane-oxidizing bacteria can acquire copper using methanobactin for particulate methane monooxygenase. Work in Methylosinus trichosporium OB3b identified the copper-binding protein MbnP and its unusual high-affinity Cu(I) site.
In E. coli, copper rapidly inactivated iron-sulfur dehydratases involved in amino-acid synthesis; this damage occurred without oxygen and released iron from exposed clusters.
Copper export, glutathione binding, and iron-sulfur cluster repair increased resistance in the E. coli experiments, illustrating how metal trafficking determines toxicity.

microbiome.text: These examples establish biochemical mechanisms in cultured microbes. They do not demonstrate that a given copper exposure changes a human gut community, or that detecting copper-resistance genes predicts the direction of that change.

exposure.text: Copper availability depends on binding and trafficking, so culture-medium copper and copper at intracellular targets are distinct quantities.

limits.text: The iron-sulfur damage was oxygen-independent. Community-level extrapolation requires speciation and species-specific measurements.

name: Zinc
role: Nutrient limitation, metal competition, and colonization resistance

summary.text: Zinc is a microbial nutrient whose excess can also impair other metal-dependent processes. Its effects depend on the balance between accessible zinc and competing nutrients, not simply on the amount of zinc present.

mechanisms.text: In Streptococcus pneumoniae, extracellular Zn(II) competes with Mn(II) for the uptake protein PsaA. Zinc binding can block manganese acquisition and weaken oxidative-stress resistance.
Host calprotectin limits metal availability. Experiments with C. difficile established zinc-sensitive growth and a protective role for calprotectin-mediated metal restriction.
Excess dietary zinc altered mouse gut community composition, lowered the antibiotic exposure needed to permit C. difficile infection, and increased disease severity in that experimental model.

microbiome.text: The strongest causal community-level example highlighted here is an animal study, rather than a human supplementation trial. The mouse C. difficile findings show that nutrient availability can change colonization resistance, but do not establish an equivalent threshold or response in humans.

exposure.text: Dietary zinc and host redistribution of zinc at infection sites create distinct microbial exposures. Zinc-to-manganese balance was mechanistically important in the pneumococcal culture experiments.

limits.text: Zinc-driven manganese starvation is demonstrated for particular transport machinery. It should not be generalized to all species, and the mouse infection findings do not define a clinical intake recommendation.

summary.text: Molybdenum enables microbial reactions through specialized cofactors, including respiratory molybdoenzymes and the distinct FeMo cofactor of nitrogenase. These pathways connect metal availability with anaerobic growth and environmental nitrogen cycling.

mechanisms.text: During experimental intestinal inflammation, host-derived nitrate gave E. coli a respiratory growth advantage over obligate anaerobes in mice.
Molybdenum-cofactor-dependent respiratory pathways supported inflammation-associated Enterobacteriaceae expansion; tungstate interfered with these pathways in culture and mouse experiments.
The common nitrogenase contains an FeMo cofactor. Comparison with vanadium nitrogenase demonstrates that replacing the heterometal changes cofactor structure and catalytic properties.

microbiome.text: The gut evidence highlighted here comes from mouse inflammation models and bacterial genetic experiments. It establishes a role for respiratory metabolism, not a demonstration that dietary molybdenum causes inflammatory bowel disease in people.

exposure.text: Molybdenum-containing cofactors must be assembled within the organism; an environmental or dietary total-metal measurement does not establish the amount entering active respiratory enzymes.

limits.text: Respiratory advantage depends on electron acceptors and local conditions. Gene presence, total molybdenum, and molybdoenzyme activity are separate measurements.

summary.text: Tungsten is a functional cofactor in some microbes, including gut-associated organisms. It also competes with molybdenum-dependent pathways, so its effect depends on which metal-utilizing enzymes a species possesses.

mechanisms.text: Purified tungsten-containing oxidoreductases from gut microbes converted aldehydes to acids. Genomic analysis identified diverse enzyme families and the tungstate-specific transporter Tup in the human gut microbiome.
One characterized enzyme coupled aldehyde oxidation to reduction of both NAD+ and ferredoxin through electron bifurcation.

The human-fecal isolate Brevibacillus massiliensis produced a tungsten enzyme that oxidized food-associated aldehydes; furfural conversion required tungsten rather than molybdenum in the tested culture conditions.
Tungstate inhibited molybdenum-dependent respiration and reduced inflammation-associated Enterobacteriaceae expansion in mouse colitis models.

microbiome.text: Tungstoenzyme work establishes biochemical capacity in cultured gut isolates and genomic potential in human microbiomes. The colitis work is preclinical; it does not establish the safety or effectiveness of tungsten administration in humans.

exposure.text: The aldehyde studies connect microbial tungsten availability with metabolism of compounds found in cooked foods or produced by microbes. They do not establish a human dietary tungsten requirement.

limits.text: Not every tungsten oxidoreductase has a known substrate. An enzyme's presence should not be treated as evidence that tungsten exposure improves health.

summary.text: Beryllium is included as a mechanistic edge case rather than a well-established microbiome exposure field. It is a light alkaline-earth metal, not a heavy metal.

mechanisms.text: A biochemical study found that beryllium sulfate inhibited alkaline phosphatase, including the Escherichia coli enzyme; sensitivity differed sharply among the enzymes tested.

microbiome.text: The evidence cited here is enzyme-level. It does not establish a beryllium-specific microbial community change in the human gut.

exposure.text: The relevant experiment used soluble beryllium sulfate. It cannot represent every beryllium-containing material or exposure route.

limits.text: This older, narrow mechanistic result supports inclusion in a research map, but not broad claims about disease mediation, microbial nutrition, or clinical treatment.

summary.text: Aluminum belongs in a broad microbial metals guide even though it is a light metal. Its relevance here is experimental exposure biology rather than an established microbial nutrient role.

mechanisms.text: In an eight-week oral-exposure study, aluminum altered selected bacterial abundances in mice without the significant overall diversity decline seen with copper in the same experiment.

microbiome.text: The study reported increased Odoribacter and decreased Anaerotruncus, alongside a reduction in Akkermansia shared across the tested metals.

exposure.text: Interpretation requires the aluminum compound, dose, duration, and route. The cited evidence is a controlled mouse ingestion experiment.

limits.text: Individual taxon changes in mice do not establish an aluminum-specific human microbiome signature, disease causation, or a clinical detoxification strategy.

sources.title: Effects of subchronic oral toxic metal exposure on the intestinal microbiota of mice
sources.authors: Zhai Q, Li T, Yu L et al.

summary.text: Chromium must be described by oxidation state. Microbial reduction of chromate, Cr(VI), changes its chemistry, but reduction is not equivalent to making all chromium harmless.

mechanisms.text: An Escherichia coli flavin-reductase system converted chromate into a soluble Cr(III)-NAD+ complex in biochemical experiments.
Reduced chromium can remain associated with cellular ligands rather than simply precipitating; the location and products of reduction matter.

microbiome.text: Five-day exposures to several metals, including chromium, elicited different rat gut-community responses. Large variation limited conclusions from diversity measures.

exposure.text: Chromate and dichromate salts used in experiments represent Cr(VI), which should not be conflated with Cr(III), elemental chromium, or chromium in an alloy.

limits.text: Enzyme and rat studies establish mechanisms and experimental responses; they do not prove that a particular human microbiome change mediates chromium disease or supports chromium supplementation.

sources.authors: Puzon GJ, Petersen JN, Roberts AG et al.

sources.authors: Richardson JB, Dancy BCR, Horton CL et al.

summary.text: Germanium is a metalloid with experimentally documented effects on microbial growth.

mechanisms.text: Tests in 21 bacterial and 13 yeast strains found substantial differences in tolerance to germanium dioxide. Prior exposure improved tolerance in some bacterial cultures.

microbiome.text: This is isolate-level evidence; it does not identify a characteristic human microbiome signature.

exposure.text: The tested form was GeO₂ in broth. Medium pH changed tolerance and may explain part of the yeast inhibition.

limits.text: Do not transfer results between inorganic germanium, organogermanium compounds, and supplements, or between a culture concentration and an environmental dose.

sources.authors: Van Dyke MI, Lee H and Trevors JT

summary.text: Arsenic illustrates a two-way relationship: microbial transformations change the compounds a host encounters, while the microbiome can alter arsenic excretion and toxicity.

mechanisms.text: Human colon communities in a gut simulator methylated and thiolated inorganic arsenic. Products included MMA(III); methylation therefore cannot automatically be labeled detoxification.
In acute-exposure mouse models, removing or disrupting the microbiome reduced fecal arsenic excretion and increased tissue accumulation. Protection also depended on the host As3mt enzyme.

microbiome.text: A study of 204 infants found exposure-associated differences in gut composition, including sex-specific patterns. This was observational and did not establish that the microbiome caused disease.

exposure.text: Food, drinking water, and contaminated soil can deliver different arsenicals. Inorganic As(III), As(V), and methylated or sulfur-containing metabolites must be distinguished.

limits.text: Gut-simulator chemistry, acute mouse toxicity, and human cohort associations answer different questions. None establishes a general probiotic treatment or a universal arsenic-associated microbial signature.

name: Cadmium
role: Toxicant with a specialized algal enzyme exception

summary.text: Cadmium is studied as a gut toxicant, but its biology is not uniformly nonfunctional: certain marine diatoms can use it in carbonic anhydrase under zinc limitation.

mechanisms.text: Germ-free mice absorbed and accumulated more orally administered cadmium than conventional mice, implicating the microbiota and host intestinal metal-handling responses.
Thalassiosira weissflogii produces a cadmium-containing carbonic anhydrase involved in inorganic-carbon acquisition. This narrow adaptation is not evidence that cadmium is a human nutrient.

microbiome.text: Oral cadmium exposure produced modest, taxon-specific shifts in a mouse sequencing study; effects should not be converted into a fixed human dysbiosis signature.

exposure.text: The gut experiments used soluble cadmium salts by oral exposure. The diatom result concerns low-zinc marine culture conditions.

limits.text: Dose, metal availability, zinc status, and species determine the result. Mouse absorption data and marine algal biochemistry cannot establish clinical benefit or a safe dietary dose.

summary.text: Tin–microbe interactions are strongly compound-dependent. Organotins such as tributyltin require separate treatment from inorganic tin.

mechanisms.text: Some sulfate- and nitrate-reducing isolates transformed tributyltin by removing organic groups under anoxic culture conditions.
Desulfobulbus propionicus also methylated inorganic tin into more toxic organotin forms. Microbial transformation therefore need not mean detoxification.

microbiome.text: The cited work examines anaerobic environmental isolates and tin speciation rather than the human gut microbiome.

exposure.text: Experiments used environmentally relevant tributyltin concentrations and isotope-enriched inorganic tin to distinguish dealkylation from methylation.

limits.text: Several tested Desulfovibrio strains did not transform tin under the same study conditions. Neither a genus name nor a decline in one tin species establishes total removal.

name: Antimony
role: Microbial redox transformations in contaminated environments

summary.text: Antimony is a metalloid whose oxidation state can be changed by bacteria. Its microbial literature is particularly relevant to mine-impacted sediments and environmental mobility.

mechanisms.text: Genetic and enzyme experiments identified AnoA as an NADP+-dependent antimonite-oxidizing enzyme in Agrobacterium tumefaciens; deleting the gene reduced, but did not eliminate, Sb(III) oxidation.
Bacteria isolated from contaminated mine sediments oxidized Sb(III) with oxygen or nitrate under the tested conditions.

microbiome.text: These studies concern environmental isolates and redox physiology, not a demonstrated antimony-specific signature in the human gut.

exposure.text: Antimonite, Sb(III), and antimonate, Sb(V), must be distinguished. The sediment setting connects microbial activity to antimony cycling at contamination sites.

limits.text: A transformation can change mobility and toxicity without removing total antimony. Culture capabilities do not establish field remediation performance or human clinical effects.

sources.authors: Li J, Wang Q, Li M et al.

sources.authors: Terry LR, Kulp TR, Wiatrowski H et al.

summary.text: Tellurite is a potent microbial stressor, and reduction to elemental tellurium is one experimentally demonstrated route of tolerance.

mechanisms.text: In Escherichia coli, intracellular reduced thiols were linked to tellurite reduction. Reduction increased under anaerobic conditions and contributed to resistance.

microbiome.text: This is evidence from bacterial physiology, not proof of a tellurium-driven disease microbiome in people.

exposure.text: The experiments used the oxyanion tellurite, Te(IV). Elemental tellurium, tellurate, and engineered particles require separate characterization.

limits.text: Resistance varies with cellular redox state and oxygen conditions. A bacterium that makes elemental tellurium is not automatically suitable for human use or unrestricted environmental deployment.

sources.authors: Muñoz-Diaz P, Jiménez K, Luraschi R et al.

summary.text: Microbes can both generate methylmercury in environmental systems and help remove its methyl group in the gut. These processes have different genes, settings, and consequences.

mechanisms.text: Deleting either hgcA or hgcB abolished mercury methylation in two tested anaerobic bacteria, providing a genetic foundation for environmental methylmercury production.

In a coordinated human and gnotobiotic-mouse study, stool demethylation activity correlated with methylmercury elimination. The human microbiomes lacked the conventional merB pathway, leaving the responsible mechanism unresolved.

microbiome.text: The 27-person study found variable elimination and mixed responses to a prebiotic. Transplanted human communities restored elimination in germ-free mice, but one associated species alone did not.

exposure.text: Methylmercury in contaminated fish is a distinct exposure from inorganic Hg(II) or elemental Hg(0); total mercury alone does not capture these differences.

limits.text: A methylation gene indicates potential, not the rate of methylmercury production in a particular sample. These findings do not support a standardized microbiome detox regimen.

summary.text: Thallium has both animal microbiome and environmental community evidence, with strong dependence on exposure conditions and ecological setting.

mechanisms.text: In mice, two weeks of Tl(I) exposure changed regional intestinal bacterial abundances and metabolites and altered local immune measurements.
At a thallium-bearing pyrite mine, microbial distributions covaried with thallium fractions and iron, manganese, and sulfur cycling.

microbiome.text: The mouse study found changes in within-sample diversity but limited effects on between-sample diversity; the gut response was not uniform along the digestive tract.

exposure.text: Tl(I) in a controlled exposure and mixed mine-soil geochemistry represent different causal questions. Co-occurring metals, pH, and depth can shape field associations.

limits.text: Mouse correlations between metabolites and bacteria do not establish mediation. Field co-occurrence does not prove that a specific taxon directly transforms thallium.

summary.text: Lead exposure and gut ecology can influence one another: animal experiments show both community changes after exposure and altered absorption when the microbiota is absent.

mechanisms.text: After six weeks of oral exposure, germ-free mice had greater lead absorption and distribution into blood and organs than conventionally colonized animals.
Host intestinal metal-handling genes also differed, implicating microbial and host processes.

microbiome.text: A separate mouse study found specific community shifts after oral lead exposure, rather than a uniform disappearance of the microbiota.

exposure.text: The experiments used oral lead salts and do not represent every exposure route or material.

limits.text: Animal findings do not identify a clinical diagnostic microbiome signature or show that a probiotic prevents lead-related disease.

name: Titanium
role: Nanoparticle exposure and soil nitrogen cycling

summary.text: Titanium–microbe research includes oxide nanoparticles and engineered surfaces. These forms need separate interpretation.

mechanisms.text: A 90-day agricultural-soil experiment with titanium dioxide nanoparticles found reduced nitrification activity and ammonia-oxidizer abundance, alongside changes in bacterial community structure.

microbiome.text: The evidence includes soil bacteria and archaea. It does not establish a human gut or disease outcome.

exposure.text: The soil experiment tested 1 and 500 mg/kg dry soil. Particle properties, concentration, and soil chemistry are central to exposure interpretation.

limits.text: Results from this soil and nanoparticle preparation cannot represent every titanium-containing pigment, implant, or food exposure.

sources.title: Titanium dioxide nanoparticles strongly impact soil microbial function by affecting archaeal nitrifiers
sources.authors: Simonin M et al.

summary.text: Gallium can enter bacterial iron-handling pathways and disrupt iron-dependent functions. This makes metal recognition itself an antimicrobial target.

mechanisms.text: In Pseudomonas aeruginosa, gallium inhibited growth and biofilms, reduced iron uptake, and interfered with iron-responsive regulation; added iron could weaken its effect.
Experiments in cystic-fibrosis sputum and mice linked gallium to inhibition of iron-dependent enzymes and increased sensitivity to oxidants.

microbiome.text: An early phase 1 trial in people with cystic fibrosis and chronic P. aeruginosa infection reported a lung-function signal. This was a preliminary clinical study, not a community-wide microbiome treatment.

exposure.text: The antimicrobial studies used specified gallium formulations, including gallium nitrate, under controlled dosing. Environmental gallium is a separate exposure question.

limits.text: Clinical efficacy, repeated-dose safety, and effects on commensal organisms cannot be inferred from culture inhibition or an early phase trial alone.

sources.title: The transition metal gallium disrupts Pseudomonas aeruginosa iron metabolism and has antimicrobial and antibiofilm activity
sources.authors: Kaneko Y, Thoendel M, Olakanmi O et al.

sources.title: Gallium disrupts bacterial iron metabolism and has therapeutic effects in mice and humans with lung infections
sources.authors: Goss CH, Kaneko Y, Khuu L et al.

summary.text: Zirconium is studied in microbial adhesion to zirconia, a ceramic used in dental materials.

mechanisms.text: A study of 12 volunteers compared biofilms forming on zirconia and titanium discs worn in oral splints for up to five days.

microbiome.text: Biofilm age influenced community composition, while the material generally did not. Volume and live/dead ratios also showed no significant material effect at the measured time points.

exposure.text: This was a human oral-surface exposure model, not an experiment with dissolved zirconium ions.

limits.text: The findings do not establish equivalence for all surface finishes or long-term implants. They also caution against calling zirconia intrinsically antimicrobial.

sources.title: Biofilm formation on zirconia and titanium over time-An in vivo model study
sources.authors: Desch A et al.

summary.text: Niobium compounds are being investigated for antimicrobial materials, with important negative results alongside promising assays.

mechanisms.text: Ammoniacal niobium oxalate inhibited bacterial growth and reduced metabolic activity in mature biofilms in laboratory tests.

microbiome.text: However, films containing the compound did not prevent adhesion and biofilm growth on titanium in the tested multispecies flow model.

exposure.text: The study tested a defined niobium compound and surface formulation, not bulk niobium as an antibiotic.

limits.text: Activity in a suspension assay did not translate into an effective antibiofilm coating. Surface retention, formulation, and community behavior need independent testing.

sources.title: Niobium-Based Conditioning Layer to Reduce Bacterial Adhesion and Biofilm Formation on Titanium Surface
sources.authors: Oliveira VC et al.

summary.text: Some ruthenium complexes inhibit bacteria in culture; their ligands are part of the active chemical system.

mechanisms.text: Ruthenium half-sandwich complexes with carbohydrate-derived ligands were tested against resistant Gram-positive isolates, including Staphylococcus and Enterococcus.

microbiome.text: Activity depended on the compound and organism. A culture assay is not evidence of improved community function.

exposure.text: These are synthesized coordination complexes rather than environmental ruthenium exposure.

limits.text: Preclinical activity does not establish a clinically usable antibiotic or the safety of ruthenium in general.

sources.title: Targeting Multiresistant Gram-Positive Bacteria by Ruthenium, Osmium, Iridium and Rhodium Half-Sandwich Type Complexes With Bidentate Monosaccharide Ligands
sources.authors: Balázs B et al.

summary.text: Rhodium is investigated as part of experimental antimicrobial coordination compounds.

mechanisms.text: Conjugating valproate to rhodium and iridium half-sandwich complexes changed their activity against S. aureus and Enterococcus faecium in culture.

microbiome.text: The work concerns selected Gram-positive organisms, not a whole-community response.

exposure.text: The ligand and organometallic fragment were tested together; the effect cannot be attributed to free rhodium alone.

limits.text: These results support further compound development, not use of rhodium or valproate as a microbiome treatment.

sources.title: Novel valproate half-sandwich rhodium and iridium conjugates to fight against multidrug-resistant Gram-positive bacteria
sources.authors: Marco A et al.

summary.text: Silver ions can disrupt several bacterial functions at once. Ionic silver, metallic silver, and silver nanoparticles are different experimental materials and should not be treated as interchangeable.

mechanisms.text: Silver disturbed disulfide-bond formation, metabolism, iron homeostasis, and membrane permeability in Gram-negative bacteria.
In culture and selected mouse infection models, silver increased the activity of several antibiotics, including against biofilm-associated cells.

microbiome.text: These experiments targeted pathogens and infection models rather than establishing beneficial remodeling of a healthy human microbiome.

exposure.text: Concentration, formulation, medium, and delivery route determine the relevant exposure; a laboratory silver-ion preparation is not equivalent to an oral silver product.

limits.text: Preclinical antibiotic enhancement is not evidence that ingesting colloidal silver is effective or safe. Antimicrobial activity alone does not establish selectivity for pathogens over commensals.

sources.title: Silver enhances antibiotic activity against gram-negative bacteria
sources.authors: Morones-Ramirez JR, Winkler JA, Spina CS et al.

summary.text: Hafnium illustrates why a material’s shape can matter as much as its elemental composition.

mechanisms.text: Engineered hafnium nanostructures reduced bacterial viability in surface experiments with S. aureus and E. coli. Flat hafnium oxide films were not significantly antibacterial relative to the control.

microbiome.text: These are two-species surface assays, not evidence of a beneficial change in a human microbial community.

exposure.text: No hafnium leaching was detected in the study; the results support a topography-related mechanism in the tested coatings.

limits.text: The measurements do not show that soluble hafnium or all hafnium surfaces kill bacteria, or that the coatings prevent clinical implant infections.

sources.title: Characterization and Antimicrobial Activity of Hafnium Nanostructures Fabricated by Physical Vapor Deposition Through a Colloidal Mask
sources.authors: Boden et al.

name: Tantalum
role: Host cells, bacteria, and implant surfaces

summary.text: Tantalum research asks how implant surfaces affect the competition between bacterial attachment and host-cell colonization.

mechanisms.text: Polished tantalum showed a lower infectious state than titanium in an animal implant model, but was not superior in direct bacterial adhesion or antibacterial assays in vitro.

microbiome.text: Cell–bacteria–material experiments suggested that host-cell attachment and subsequent detachment could help explain the difference.

exposure.text: The relevant exposure is an implanted surface, with host tissue present, rather than a dietary metal dose.

limits.text: This evidence does not make all tantalum surfaces inherently bactericidal or establish a general human infection-prevention benefit.

sources.title: Why Is Tantalum Less Susceptible to Bacterial Infection?
sources.authors: Chen X et al.

summary.text: Rhenium carbonyl complexes show how charge and molecular structure can change antibacterial activity.

mechanisms.text: A screen of di- and tricarbonyl diimine complexes found active candidates but no bactericidal or bacteriostatic activity for the tested dicarbonyl or neutral tricarbonyl species.

microbiome.text: The study used a panel of microorganisms, not human microbiome outcomes.

exposure.text: Computational docking suggested membrane-associated protein targets in S. aureus; those predictions are not direct proof of target engagement.

limits.text: Results apply to the defined complexes. Clinical effectiveness and broad ecological consequences remain separate questions.

sources.title: Antimicrobial Activity of Rhenium Di- and Tricarbonyl Diimine Complexes: Insights on Membrane-Bound S. aureus Protein Binding
sources.authors: Schindler K et al.

summary.text: Osmium appears in early antimicrobial discovery through defined organometallic complexes.

mechanisms.text: In one structure–activity study, quinoline-containing osmium complexes inhibited growth of multidrug-resistant Gram-positive bacteria.

microbiome.text: The study tested isolates rather than an intact microbiome.

exposure.text: The tested complexes cannot stand in for elemental osmium or other osmium compounds.

limits.text: Bacteriostasis in culture does not demonstrate treatment efficacy, selectivity in a complex community, or a safe human exposure.

sources.title: Half sandwich-type osmium, ruthenium, iridium and rhodium complexes with bidentate glycosyl heterocyclic ligands induce cytostasis in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer cells and bacteriostasis in Gram-positive multiresistant bacteria
sources.authors: Kacsir I et al.

summary.text: Iridium complexes are being explored as tools to disrupt bacterial biofilms.

mechanisms.text: A 2026 study reported that one cyclometalated complex damaged membranes and DNA and disrupted extracellular DNA in Gram-positive biofilms.

microbiome.text: The selected complex also reduced S. aureus biofilm infection in a mouse wound model. This goes beyond culture evidence but remains preclinical.

exposure.text: The study used a synthesized complex and topical experimental treatment; it did not test dietary iridium.

limits.text: Compound-specific results do not establish clinical safety, effectiveness in humans, or an antimicrobial property shared by all iridium compounds.

sources.title: Cyclometalated Iridium(III) Complexes with eDNA-Degrading Activity for Combating Gram-Positive Bacterial Biofilms
sources.authors: Li Y et al.

summary.text: Bismuth provides a direct example of disrupting a microbial metalloenzyme by replacing its normal metal cofactors.

mechanisms.text: Structural experiments showed one Bi(III) ion displacing two zinc ions from tested metallo-β-lactamases, enzymes that otherwise destroy certain antibiotics.
Colloidal bismuth subcitrate restored meropenem activity against metallo-β-lactamase-positive bacteria in culture and a mouse infection model.

microbiome.text: This work addresses antibiotic-resistant pathogens. It does not establish a favorable effect on overall human microbiome composition.

exposure.text: The findings concern particular bismuth compounds, including a drug used against H. pylori, and cannot be assigned to every bismuth material.

limits.text: The 2018 enzyme and mouse results support a repurposing hypothesis, not proof that a bismuth–carbapenem combination is an established clinical treatment for these infections.

sources.title: Bismuth antimicrobial drugs serve as broad-spectrum metallo-β-lactamase inhibitors
sources.authors: Wang R, Lai TP, Gao P et al.

summary.text: Scandium can change microbial secondary metabolism under laboratory conditions. It is a rare-earth element, but not a lanthanide.

mechanisms.text: Adding scandium to Bacillus subtilis cultures increased transcription linked to amylase and bacilysin production.
Scandium and/or lanthanum also activated secondary-metabolite gene clusters in Streptomyces coelicolor, with some compounds detectable only after treatment.

microbiome.text: These are culture and gene-expression findings rather than a demonstrated benefit to a human microbial community.

exposure.text: The studies supplied specified rare-earth compounds in growth media. Concentration and culture conditions determine the observed response.

limits.text: Inducing metabolite production does not establish a nutritional requirement, identify a universal cofactor role, or show that scandium supplementation is beneficial.

sources.title: Scandium stimulates the production of amylase and bacilysin in Bacillus subtilis
sources.authors: Inaoka T, Ochi K

sources.title: Rare earth elements activate the secondary metabolite-biosynthetic gene clusters in Streptomyces coelicolor A3(2)
sources.authors: Tanaka Y, Hosaka T, Ochi K

summary.text: Yttrium is studied in microbial biosorption and rare-earth recovery. Binding to biomass is distinct from use as an enzyme cofactor.

mechanisms.text: Serratia marcescens biomass removed yttrium ions from experimental wastewater through processes consistent with ion exchange, electrostatic attraction, and complexation.
Spectroscopic analyses implicated hydroxyl, carboxyl, and amino groups as metal-binding sites.

microbiome.text: The evidence concerns a wastewater biosorbent, not a human microbiome response.

exposure.text: Adsorption depended on pH, initial yttrium concentration, biomass dose, contact time, and other experimental conditions.

limits.text: Sorption does not demonstrate a requirement for yttrium or justify adding this organism to people or releasing it into the environment.

sources.title: Removal of yttrium from rare-earth wastewater by Serratia marcescens: biosorption optimization and mechanisms studies
sources.authors: Liang CL, Shen JL

name: Lanthanum
role: Cofactor in selected bacterial alcohol dehydrogenases

summary.text: Lanthanum can be a functional enzyme cofactor in certain methylotrophic bacteria, rather than merely an environmental toxicant.

mechanisms.text: Purified ExaF from Methylobacterium extorquens AM1 preferentially bound La(III) over calcium and supported oxidation of alcohol substrates.

microbiome.text: This is a specialized microbial-metabolism result; it does not establish a lanthanum requirement for the human gut community.

exposure.text: The experiments supplied La(III) in defined culture medium and measured enzyme function.

limits.text: An enzyme cofactor in one lineage is not a universal nutrient requirement. Metal binding, growth support, and host benefit are distinct endpoints.

sources.title: Pyrroloquinoline Quinone Ethanol Dehydrogenase in Methylobacterium extorquens AM1 Extends Lanthanide-Dependent Metabolism to Multicarbon Substrates
sources.authors: Good NM, Vu HN, Suriano CJ et al.

summary.text: Cerium belongs to the light lanthanides used by selected methane-oxidizing bacteria in the methanol-oxidation step of their metabolism.

mechanisms.text: Work with Methylacidiphilum fumariolicum SolV linked lanthanide-dependent growth to an XoxF-type methanol dehydrogenase containing a lanthanide cofactor.

microbiome.text: The organism came from a volcanic mudpot; these findings concern environmental carbon cycling.

exposure.text: Dissolved Ce(III) available to enzymes must be distinguished from cerium-oxide particles and other cerium formulations.

limits.text: This mechanism does not establish a human nutritional requirement or predict the behavior of every cerium-containing material.

sources.title: Rare earth metals are essential for methanotrophic life in volcanic mudpots
sources.authors: Pol A, Barends TR, Dietl A et al.

summary.text: Praseodymium can support a lanthanide-dependent alcohol dehydrogenase in a soil bacterium, extending the biology beyond methane specialists.

mechanisms.text: Purified PedH from Pseudomonas putida KT2440 was active with Pr(III) and several other light lanthanides; its calcium-dependent counterpart is PedE.

microbiome.text: The evidence concerns defined enzymes and bacterial cultures, not demonstrated effects on a human microbiome.

exposure.text: The active species in these experiments was a supplied trivalent lanthanide ion.

limits.text: Activity with Pr(III) does not mean every bacterium requires praseodymium or that replacing another metal always improves activity.

sources.title: Functional Role of Lanthanides in Enzymatic Activity and Transcriptional Regulation of Pyrroloquinoline Quinone-Dependent Alcohol Dehydrogenases in Pseudomonas putida KT2440
sources.authors: Wehrmann M, Billard P, Martin-Meriadec A et al.

summary.text: Neodymium has been directly located in the active site of a functional bacterial methanol dehydrogenase.

mechanisms.text: XoxF1 purified from Methylacidimicrobium thermophilum AP8 grown with neodymium was characterized by crystallography and enzyme kinetics.
A separate Methylorubrum extorquens study found preference for lanthanum over neodymium, showing that light lanthanides are not interchangeable in every enzyme.

microbiome.text: These are studies of methylotrophic or methanotrophic isolates and environmental metabolism.

exposure.text: Experiments used Nd(III) supplied in controlled media; alloy particles and other neodymium-bearing materials require separate evaluation.

limits.text: Cofactor activity demonstrates a specific biochemical function, not a human health benefit or a universal community requirement.

sources.title: Neodymium as Metal Cofactor for Biological Methanol Oxidation: Structure and Kinetics of an XoxF1-Type Methanol Dehydrogenase
sources.authors: Schmitz RA, Picone N, Singer H et al.

sources.title: Preference for particular lanthanide species and thermal stability of XoxFs in Methylorubrum extorquens strain AM1
sources.authors: Wang L, Hibino A, Suganuma S et al.

summary.text: Gadolinium shows that a microbe’s capacity to use a lanthanide can change through adaptation; this is not a fixed property shared by all bacteria.

mechanisms.text: An evolved Methylorubrum extorquens AM1 variant grew on methanol with gadolinium and accumulated the metal in an intracellular compartment.

microbiome.text: The result came from a selected laboratory variant with broad transcriptional changes, not a demonstrated general function of human gut bacteria.

exposure.text: The variant also acquired gadolinium from gadopentetic acid in experiments, connecting microbial acquisition to one contrast-agent complex.

limits.text: Acquisition from a chelate in culture does not establish its breakdown or safety profile in a person, nor justify using bacteria to treat gadolinium exposure.

sources.title: Hyperaccumulation of Gadolinium by Methylorubrum extorquens AM1 Reveals Impacts of Lanthanides on Cellular Processes Beyond Methylotrophy
sources.authors: Good NM, Lee HD, Hawker ER et al.

name: Other lanthanides
role: Comparative enzyme chemistry and evidence gaps

summary.text: Samarium, europium, terbium, dysprosium, holmium, erbium, thulium, ytterbium, and lutetium belong in the comparative lanthanide question, but evidence of enzyme binding must not be confused with established biological necessity.

mechanisms.text: A methanol-dehydrogenase study tested the lanthanide series except promethium. Earlier lanthanides supported greater activity than later members, linking ionic properties to catalytic performance.

microbiome.text: The evidence highlighted here is purified-enzyme biochemistry; it is not a demonstrated disease-associated human microbial signature.

exposure.text: Comparisons concern trivalent ions in controlled assays. Promethium was not tested and should not acquire a biological role by analogy.

limits.text: A measurable in vitro effect cannot establish that an element supports growth in nature. Separate uptake, enzyme, growth, and environmental measurements are needed.

sources.title: Impact of the lanthanide contraction on the activity of a lanthanide-dependent methanol dehydrogenase – a kinetic and DFT study
sources.authors: Lumpe H, Pol A, Op den Camp HJM, Daumann LJ

summary.text: Strontium connects urease-producing bacteria with biomineralization: microbial activity can move dissolved strontium into carbonate minerals.

mechanisms.text: A marine Bacillus isolate formed strontium-containing carbonate minerals in saline culture; microscopy also detected early cellular phosphate deposits.

microbiome.text: This is an environmental remediation experiment using a marine isolate rather than a study of human intestinal communities.

exposure.text: The work was motivated by radiostrontium contamination and tested the chemistry of Sr incorporation under controlled salinity.

limits.text: Mineral immobilization does not destroy a radionuclide. Culture performance cannot establish long-term field stability or a clinical role for the organism.

sources.title: Removal of Soluble Strontium via Incorporation into Biogenic Carbonate Minerals by Halophilic Bacterium Bacillus sp. Strain TK2d in a Highly Saline Solution
sources.authors: Horiike T, Dotsuta Y, Nakano Y et al.

summary.text: Technetium–microbe research concerns the fate of radioactive contaminants under reducing conditions.

mechanisms.text: Geobacter sulfurreducens reduced Tc(VII) directly with hydrogen as an electron donor. It also generated Fe(II)-bearing minerals that reduced technetium indirectly and promoted precipitation.

microbiome.text: The selected study includes cultures and contaminated-sediment systems, not a human gut pathway.

exposure.text: Technetium oxidation state, iron mineral form, electron donors, and local redox conditions determine the observed process.

limits.text: Reduction or precipitation changes chemical mobility; it does not remove radioactivity. Long-term stability needs testing under changing environmental conditions.

sources.title: Direct and Fe(II)-mediated reduction of technetium by Fe(III)-reducing bacteria
sources.authors: Lloyd JR et al.

summary.text: Some bacteria reduce Pd(II) to elemental palladium, linking respiratory metabolism to metal recovery and catalyst synthesis.

mechanisms.text: In Shewanella oneidensis, pyruvate increased palladium reduction compared with lactate; hydrogenases and the Mtr electron-transfer pathway contributed.
The response involved changes in carbon metabolism and gene expression, showing why the electron donor can alter an apparent metal-reduction phenotype.

microbiome.text: This is a cultured environmental model organism, not a human microbiome intervention.

exposure.text: The study used soluble Pd(II) under controlled conditions. Bulk palladium and engineered palladium particles pose different questions.

limits.text: Biogenic particles are products of microbial chemistry; their formation does not establish that palladium is a natural required cofactor or a clinically useful antimicrobial.

sources.title: Pyruvate accelerates palladium reduction by regulating catabolism and electron transfer pathway in Shewanella oneidensis
sources.authors: Cheng YY, Wang WJ, Ding ST et al.

summary.text: Indium connects microbial metabolism to recovery of technology-critical metals from discarded screens.

mechanisms.text: Adapted Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans enabled indium extraction from waste OLED touch screens under optimized acidic bioleaching conditions.

microbiome.text: The selected evidence concerns a bacterial process in a recovery system, not a human microbiome intervention.

exposure.text: Ferrous sulfate, sulfur, pH, and solid loading affected extraction. Solubilizing a metal is a process step rather than proof that the microbe requires it.

limits.text: Recovery performance under controlled conditions does not establish safety of the resulting solution or a universal extraction yield for mixed electronic waste.

sources.title: Bioleaching of critical metals from waste OLED touch screens using adapted acidophilic bacteria
sources.authors: Pourhossein F et al.

summary.text: Cesium can enter bacteria through systems that normally handle potassium. Its microbial relevance includes transport selectivity and contaminated-soil research.

mechanisms.text: Bacteria from a soil conditioner accumulated Cs+ through a saturable process competitively inhibited by potassium, implicating a potassium-transport system.

microbiome.text: The study examined environmental bacterial uptake, not a validated gut-microbiome response.

exposure.text: Cs+ chemistry can inform transport research, but stable cesium and radiocesium also differ in radiological hazard; biosorption does not remove radioactivity.

limits.text: Laboratory accumulation is not the same as successful soil remediation. Competing potassium and growth conditions can change the outcome.

sources.title: Characterization of cesium uptake mediated by a potassium transport system of bacteria in a soil conditioner
sources.authors: Zhang P, Idota Y, Yano K et al.

summary.text: Barium is part of microbial mineralization biology: a marine sponge symbiont can concentrate it into intracellular minerals.

mechanisms.text: In Theonella swinhoei, Entotheonella bacteria were identified as the main barium- and arsenic-accumulating component, with minerals associated with intracellular vesicles.

microbiome.text: This is a host–microbiome interaction in a marine sponge. It should not be transferred directly to human gut physiology.

exposure.text: The study concerns accumulated mineral phases within a symbiosis; dissolved barium and insoluble barium compounds have different chemical behavior.

limits.text: The proposed protective role for the sponge does not establish that barium is a required nutrient or that similar sequestration occurs in humans.

sources.title: Sponge-associated bacteria mineralize arsenic and barium on intracellular vesicles
sources.authors: Keren R, Mayzel B, Lavy A et al.

summary.text: Platinum interacts with microbial electron-transfer systems; the strongest evidence highlighted here concerns conversion of soluble platinum complexes into reduced forms.

mechanisms.text: Experiments with Fusarium oxysporum implicated a hydrogenase in converting platinum salts into nanoparticles.
Citrobacter freundii experiments separated Pt(IV)-to-Pt(II) reduction from the subsequent formation of Pt(0), with flavins and respiratory electron-transfer pathways contributing.

microbiome.text: These are fungal and bacterial biotransformation studies, not evidence that platinum benefits a human microbial community.

exposure.text: Oxidation state and ligands matter: platinum salts, metallic particles, and platinum-containing chemotherapy agents cannot be treated as the same exposure.

limits.text: Laboratory nanoparticle production suggests materials-recovery applications. It does not establish clinical safety, ecosystem effects at ambient concentrations, or a disease mechanism.

sources.title: Bioreduction of platinum salts into nanoparticles: a mechanistic perspective
sources.authors: Govender Y, Riddin T, Gericke M et al.

sources.title: Prompting the FDH/Hases-based electron transfers during Pt(IV) reduction mediated by bio-Pd(0)
sources.authors: Wang J, Lin W, Chen Y et al.

summary.text: Soluble gold can be toxic to microbes even though metallic gold behaves differently. Some bacteria manage this exposure by converting dissolved gold into a solid form.

mechanisms.text: Delftia acidovorans secretes delftibactin, a metallophore that protects cells from soluble gold while promoting gold biomineralization.

microbiome.text: The evidence concerns a gold-associated environmental bacterium and its secreted chemistry, rather than a demonstrated human gut function.

exposure.text: Gold-chloride exposure in culture is chemically different from bulk metallic gold, gold nanoparticles, or pharmaceutical gold complexes.

limits.text: The result demonstrates one organism’s detoxification strategy. It does not show that gold is a broadly required microbial nutrient or that gold products improve microbiome health.

sources.title: Gold biomineralization by a metallophore from a gold-associated microbe
sources.authors: Johnston CW, Wyatt MA, Li X et al.

summary.text: Thorium interacts with microbial biomass through binding and mineral formation, making it relevant to radionuclide mobility and remediation research.

mechanisms.text: A Pseudomonas isolate sequestered thorium through a combination of ion exchange, complexation, and phosphate microprecipitation; cellular phosphate and carboxyl groups contributed.

microbiome.text: The study concerns a cultured environmental bacterium. It does not establish a thorium-associated human gut signature.

exposure.text: A soluble thorium exposure in a sorption experiment is distinct from thorium locked in a mineral. Chemical binding does not eliminate radiological hazard.

limits.text: Sequestration is not evidence that the bacterium respires thorium or needs it as a nutrient. Performance and stability require evaluation in the relevant environmental matrix.

sources.title: Uranium and thorium sequestration by a Pseudomonas sp.: mechanism and chemical characterization
sources.authors: Kazy SK, D'Souza SF, Sar P

summary.text: Some anaerobic microbes can obtain energy while reducing uranium. This places uranium within environmental microbial metabolism even though it is not a conventional nutrient.

mechanisms.text: Dissimilatory iron-reducing microorganisms can couple electron transport to U(VI) reduction, producing U(IV) and supporting growth.
In a separate Pseudomonas study, sequestration included ion exchange, binding to cellular groups, and phosphate microprecipitation rather than respiration alone.

microbiome.text: These studies address sediments, aquifers, and isolated organisms. They do not establish a uranium-related human gut signature.

exposure.text: U(VI) and U(IV), dissolved ligands, and mineral products determine mobility. Remediation aims to immobilize uranium rather than destroy the element.

limits.text: A successful laboratory reduction or biosorption result does not guarantee durable field containment; chemical conditions and the stability of the resulting phases remain important.

sources.title: Microbial reduction of uranium
sources.authors: Lovley DR, Phillips EJP, Gorby YA, Landa ER

sources.title: Uranium and thorium sequestration by a Pseudomonas sp.: mechanism and chemical characterization
sources.authors: Kazy SK, D'Souza SF, Sar P

summary.text: Neptunium is relevant to microbial control of radionuclide mobility.

mechanisms.text: Shewanella putrefaciens reduced Np(V), but reduction alone did not remove it from solution. Coupling reduction with phosphate liberation by a Citrobacter strain enabled removal.

microbiome.text: The evidence comes from a controlled remediation experiment, not a microbiome or health study.

exposure.text: The process depends on chemical speciation and a precipitating ligand, not simply the presence of metal-reducing bacteria.

limits.text: Immobilization must be distinguished from destruction of radioactivity. Performance under laboratory conditions does not establish durable containment in a field site.

sources.title: Biological reduction and removal of Np(V) by two microorganisms
sources.authors: Lloyd JR, Yong P and Macaskie LE

summary.text: Plutonium speciation can be changed by metal-reducing bacteria in laboratory systems.

mechanisms.text: Geobacter metallireducens and Shewanella oneidensis reduced Pu(V/VI) to Pu(IV), producing nanoparticulate aggregates associated with cells.

microbiome.text: This is environmental culture evidence. It does not demonstrate a human microbial response or nutritional function.

exposure.text: Pu(IV) was stable under the tested conditions; Pu(III) was not observed.

limits.text: Growth supported by plutonium as the sole electron acceptor was inconclusive. Reduction is not proof of respiration, and precipitation does not eliminate radioactivity.

sources.title: Plutonium(V/VI) Reduction by the Metal-Reducing Bacteria Geobacter metallireducens GS-15 and Shewanella oneidensis MR-1
sources.authors: Icopini GA et al.

summary.text: Americium interactions with microbes are studied to understand radionuclide mobility and separation, rather than microbial nutrition.

mechanisms.text: Laboratory Escherichia coli and marine bacterial strains accumulated americium-241 in patterns dependent on pH, medium, strain, and growth stage.
Rhizopus fungal biomass adsorbed americium-241 from solution in a separate controlled study, with strong effects of solution conditions.

microbiome.text: Bacterial culture filtrates also suggested that secreted compounds could complex americium and influence its solubility. The evidence does not describe a human gut pathway.

exposure.text: The cited experiments used americium-241 in defined solutions; mineral-bound material and mixed radioactive waste require separate characterization.

limits.text: Accumulation or adsorption does not demonstrate respiration, eliminate radioactivity, or establish durable containment. A microbial process can alter mobility without destroying the element.

sources.title: Interactions of Escherichia coli and marine bacteria with 241Am in laboratory cultures
sources.authors: Wurtz EA, Sibley TH, Schell WR

sources.title: Biosorption of 241Am by Rhizopus arrihizus: preliminary investigation and evaluation
sources.authors: Liu N, Yang Y, Luo S et al.

summary.text: Lithium belongs in the broader ion–microbe picture, although it is a light alkali metal rather than a heavy metal.

mechanisms.text: Two bacterial riboswitch classes sense elevated lithium and regulate transport genes, commonly nhaA. These systems help prevent lithium toxicity, particularly at high pH.

microbiome.text: The selected study establishes bacterial sensing and gene regulation, not an effect of prescribed lithium on a human gut community.

exposure.text: Environmental lithium concentrations and pH determine the conditions under which these defenses become relevant.

limits.text: A bacterial tolerance mechanism does not establish a nutritional requirement or a clinical benefit. Community-level responses require separate measurements.

sources.title: Lithium-sensing riboswitch classes regulate expression of bacterial cation transporter genes
sources.authors: White N et al.

name: Sodium
role: Broader metal context: sodium gradients, salinity, and gut ecology

summary.text: Sodium is an alkali metal, not a heavy metal in conventional usage, but it matters for microbial energy and environmental adaptation. Salt exposure can also change host-associated communities through mechanisms that extend beyond sodium transport itself.

mechanisms.text: In Vibrio cholerae, the Na+-translocating NADH:quinone oxidoreductase contributes to sodium extrusion and membrane voltage during respiration.
A high-salt diet reduced Lactobacillus murinus in mice and altered immune-related phenotypes; a small human salt-challenge study also observed changes involving lactobacilli and TH17 cells.

microbiome.text: The salt study combined mechanistic mouse experiments with a limited human pilot. The human arm supports further investigation, while the causal disease experiments were performed in mice.

exposure.text: Dietary salt challenge, external salinity, and a bacterial sodium gradient are different quantities. Sodium chloride exposure also changes chloride and osmotic conditions.

limits.text: A salt response should not be interpreted as a generic heavy-metal effect. The pilot study does not establish a universal human microbial signature of sodium intake.

sources.title: Role of the Na(+)-translocating NADH:quinone oxidoreductase in voltage generation and Na(+) extrusion in Vibrio cholerae
sources.authors: Vorburger T et al.

sources.title: Salt-responsive gut commensal modulates TH17 axis and disease
sources.authors: Wilck N et al.

name: Magnesium
role: Broader metal context: ribosome function and magnesium sensing

summary.text: Magnesium belongs in microbial metallomics as a major cellular ion, although it is not conventionally grouped with heavy metals. It connects the physical stability of protein-synthesis machinery with bacterial sensing of the local environment.

mechanisms.text: In Salmonella, the PhoQ sensor responds to extracellular magnesium and changes expression of PhoP-regulated genes.
Low cytoplasmic magnesium destabilized Salmonella ribosomes, slowed translation, and altered ATP and phosphate balance. Increased magnesium uptake and metabolic adjustment helped restore homeostasis.

microbiome.text: These are mechanistic bacterial studies, not evidence that magnesium supplementation produces a predictable human community-wide response. They show why extracellular concentration and intracellular availability must be distinguished.

exposure.text: Defined culture-medium magnesium and intracellular free magnesium were distinct experimental variables. Bulk elemental measurements alone cannot resolve this regulatory system.

limits.text: PhoQ biology is organism-specific, and magnesium sensing is only one part of the host-environment signals affecting bacteria.

sources.title: Mg2+ as an extracellular signal: environmental regulation of Salmonella virulence
sources.authors: García Véscovi E, Soncini FC, and Groisman EA

sources.title: Protein synthesis controls phosphate homeostasis
sources.authors: Pontes MH and Groisman EA

name: Potassium
role: Broader metal context: ion homeostasis and biofilm signaling

summary.text: Potassium is a major cellular ion and an alkali metal, included here as broader metallomic context. Bacteria regulate its uptake and can use potassium flux to coordinate behavior within a biofilm.

mechanisms.text: Bacillus subtilis biofilms transmitted waves of potassium through ion channels, linking membrane depolarization with coordinated metabolic activity.

In B. subtilis, the second messenger cyclic di-AMP regulates potassium homeostasis. Genetic experiments identified KimA as a potassium importer and showed that potassium availability changes the consequences of losing c-di-AMP synthesis.

microbiome.text: These studies establish mechanisms in a model bacterium and laboratory biofilms. They do not show that dietary potassium has the same effects in a complex human gut community.

exposure.text: The experiments controlled extracellular potassium and measured bacterial responses; cellular potassium pools and gradients remain distinct from total dietary intake.

limits.text: Electrical signaling in a biofilm is a physiological observation, not evidence of cognition or a demonstrated human disease pathway.

sources.title: Ion channels enable electrical communication in bacterial communities
sources.authors: Prindle A et al.

sources.title: Control of potassium homeostasis is an essential function of the second messenger cyclic di-AMP in Bacillus subtilis
sources.authors: Gundlach J et al.

name: Calcium
role: Broader metal context: biofilm architecture and biomineralization

summary.text: Calcium is included as broader metal context rather than as a heavy metal. In some bacteria it supports organized mineral structures within biofilms, linking cellular ion handling to community architecture.

mechanisms.text: In Bacillus subtilis laboratory biofilms, a calcium-accumulating cell subpopulation initiated calcium carbonate formation that contributed to an organized mineral scaffold.
Changing calcium availability altered biofilm gene expression and structure, and inhibiting calcium uptake prevented normal development under the studied conditions.

microbiome.text: This evidence comes from laboratory B. subtilis biofilms. It does not establish that dietary calcium controls mineralization or biofilm behavior across human microbial communities.

exposure.text: Calcium salts in a defined experimental biofilm system were the relevant exposure. Dissolved calcium and precipitated calcium carbonate are different forms.

limits.text: The study did not directly establish how intracellular mineral reaches the extracellular matrix, and its importance in natural soil or host communities remains unresolved.

sources.title: The roles of intracellular and extracellular calcium in Bacillus subtilis biofilms
sources.authors: Keren-Paz A et al.

summary.text: Selenium is a nonmetal included because trace-element availability, host nutrition, and microbial transformations intersect. It is not accurately described as a heavy metal.

mechanisms.text: Thauera selenatis can respire selenate using a periplasmic reductase distinct from its nitrate-respiration system.
In mice, dietary selenium changed gut communities, while colonization reduced the selenium available for some host selenoprotein responses.

microbiome.text: The mouse study found taxon-specific effects and evidence of competition between host and microbes for selenium; more dietary selenium was not tested as a universal clinical microbiome therapy.

exposure.text: Selenate, selenite, and organic selenium compounds differ in metabolism. Dietary availability and environmental redox conditions answer different biological questions.

limits.text: Respiration in an environmental isolate and controlled mouse diets do not establish that selenium supplementation improves human microbiome health.

sources.title: The terminal reductases for selenate and nitrate respiration in Thauera selenatis are two distinct enzymes

summary.text: Rubidium is an alkali metal relevant to microbial ion selectivity, even though it is not usually the focus of heavy-metal toxicology.

mechanisms.text: The Escherichia coli Kup potassium-uptake system discriminated relatively weakly among K+, Rb+, and Cs+, demonstrating that transport pathways can admit chemically similar ions.

microbiome.text: This is a bacterial transport experiment, not a study of a rubidium-associated human microbial community.

exposure.text: The relevant variables are dissolved cations, the competing potassium supply, and the transport system present in the strain.

limits.text: Transportability is not evidence of a universal nutritional requirement or beneficial dietary supplementation. Other potassium transporters need not have identical selectivity.

sources.title: Specific cesium transport via the Escherichia coli Kup (TrkD) K+ uptake system
